images.title: Common multiples never stop
images.purpose: Show the common multiples of 6 and 8 going on for ever in steps of 24, with 24 as the lowest.
images.composition: One long horizontal number line across the middle of the frame with four marked points and equal jump arcs above, running off to the right in an arrowhead; open white space above and below.
exact_structure: One horizontal grey #6B7280 number line starting at 0 on the left and ending in an arrowhead at the right edge; the line continues past 96 with no further marks.
Exactly 5 labelled ticks, equally spaced: 0, 24, 48, 72, 96; no other ticks and no other numbers on the line.
Large dots on 24, 48, 72 and 96 only (exactly 4 dots); the dot on 24 is larger and reddish purple #CC79A7, the dots on 48, 72 and 96 are teal #0072B2.
Exactly 4 equal amber #E69F00 jump arcs above the line: 0 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 72, 72 to 96, each with the text +24 at its top.
One short dotted amber arc starting at 96 and fading toward the arrowhead, with the text goes on for ever above it.
The word LCM directly under the 24 tick, in reddish purple.
rejection: any tick or number on the line other than 0, 24, 48, 72 and 96
LCM placed under any number other than 24
the line ending in a bar or a final number instead of an arrowhead
images.takeaway: There is always a lowest common multiple, but no largest, since you can always add another 24.
images.description: A number line with common multiples 24, 48, 72 and 96 joined by +24 jumps, 24 marked LCM, and an arrow showing the list goes on for ever.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on the LCM and why there is no largest common multiple.
images.teaching_notes: Point at the arrowhead and ask what comes after 96; adding 24 again always gives another common multiple.

image_decisions.why: A number line with endless +24 jumps shows at once why there is a lowest but no largest common multiple.
